### Immunofluorescence

Timed pregnant dams were euthanized and embryos collected in ice cold PBS and then fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) (Fisher 50-980-494) for 1–2 hr at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. Embryos were then washed three times for 30 min each in PBS +0.1% Triton X-100 (Fisher 327371000) (PBTriton) at room temperature followed by a 1 hr incubation in blocking solution (PBTriton +3% BSA) at room temperature. Embryos were then incubated in staining solution (PBTriton +1.5% BSA) with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by three 30 min washes in PBTriton at room temperature. Embryos were then incubated in staining solution with Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500; Thermo Fisher) for 1 hr at room temperature, followed by three 30 min washes in PBTriton at room temperature. Embryos were stored in PBTriton at 4 °C until imaging. Primary antibodies were rat anti-E-cadherin (1:300; Sigma U3254), rabbit anti-FoxA2 (1:1000; abcam ab108422), rabbit anti N-cadherin (1:500; Cell Signaling Technology D4R1H), and mouse anti-Nkx6-1 (1:50; Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank F55A10; Pedersen et al., 2006). Secondary Alexa fluor conjugated antibodies were added along with Alexa 546-conjugated phalloidin (Molecular Probes) at a 1:1000 dilution. Embryos were washed three times for 30 min each in PBTriton at room temperature and imaged on a Zeiss LSM 900 confocal microscope.

### Confocal imaging

Whole-mount imaging was performed by mounting embryos dorsal side down in PBTriton (PBS +0.1% Triton X-100) in Attofluor cell chambers (Thermo Fisher A7816), using a small fragment of broken coverglass (Corning 2850–18) with small dabs of vacuum grease (Dow Corning DC 976) to mount the embryo on a #1.5 coverglass (Fisher 12-546-2P). Embryos were imaged by confocal microscopy on inverted microscopes on a Zeiss LSM700 equipped with a Plan-NeoFluar 40 x/1.3 objective, a Zeiss LSM900 with a Plan-NeoFluar 40 x/1.3 objective, or a Leica SP8 with an HC PL Apo 40 x/1.3 objective. Images were captured by tile-based acquisition of contiguous z-stacks of 50–150 µm depth with 0.6–1.2 µm optical slices and 0.3–0.5 µm z-steps. For tiled images, computational stitching was performed using 10% overlap per tile in Zen (Zeiss) or LAS-X (Leica) software.

Summary:

This impressive study presents a comprehensive scRNAseq atlas of the cranial region during neural induction, patterning, and morphogenesis. The authors collected a robust scRNAseq dataset covering six distinct developmental stages. The analysis focused on the neural tissue, resulting in a highly detailed temporal map of neural plate development. The findings demonstrate how different cell fates are organized in specific spatial patterns along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes within the developing neural tissue. Additionally, the research utilized high-density single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) to reveal intricate spatial and temporal patterns independent of traditional spatial techniques.

The investigation utilized diffusion component analysis to spatially order cells based on their positioning along the anterior-posterior axis, corresponding to the forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, and medial-lateral axis. By cross-referencing with MGI expression data, the identification of cell types was validated, affirming the expression patterns of numerous known genes and implicating others as differentially expressed along these axes. These findings significantly advance our understanding of the spatially regulated genes in neural tissues during early developmental stages. The emphasis on transcription factors, cell surface, and secreted proteins provides valuable insights into the intricate gene regulatory networks underpinning neural tissue patterning. Analysis of a second scRNAseq dataset where Shh signaling was inhibited by culturing embryos in SAG identified known and previously unknown transcripts regulated by Shh, including the Wnt pathway.

The data includes the neural plate and captures all major cell types in the head, including the mesoderm, endoderm, non-neural ectoderm, neural crest, notochord, and blood. With further analyses, this high-quality data promises to significantly advance our understanding of how these tissues develop in conjunction with the neural tissue, paving the way for future breakthroughs in developmental biology and genomics.

The data is well presented in the figures and thoroughly described in the text. The quality of the scRNAseq data and bioinformatic analysis is exceptional.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102819.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102819.3.sa2)

Summary:

Brooks et al. generate a compelling gene expression atlas of the early embryonic cranial neural plate. They generate single-cell transcriptome data from early cranial neural plate cells at 6 consecutive stages between E7.5 to E9. Utilizing computational analysis they infer temporal gene expression dynamics and spatial gene expression patterns along the anterior-posterior and mediolateral axis of the neural plate. Subsequent comparison with known gene expression patterns revealed a good agreement with their inferred patterns, thus validating their approach. They then focus on Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) signalling, a key morphogen signal, whose activities partition the neural plate into distinct gene expression domains along the mediolateral axis. Single-cell transcriptome analysis of embryos in which the Shh pathway was pharmacologically activated throughout the neural plate revealed characteristic changes in gene expression along the mediolateral axis and the induction of distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs in the developing fore-, mid- and hindbrain.

Strengths:

This manuscript provides a comprehensive transcriptomic characterisation of the developing cranial neural plate, a part of the embryo that to my knowledge has not been extensively analysed by single-cell transcriptomic approaches. The single-cell sequencing data appears to be of high quality and will be a great resource for the wider scientific community. Moreover, the computational analysis is well executed and the validation of the sequencing data using published gene expression patterns is convincing. In my opinion the authors completely achieved their aim of generating a reliable sequencing atlas of the early cranial neural plate. Conceptually, the findings that gene expression patterns differ along the rostrocaudal, mediolateral and temporal axes of the neural plate and that Shh signalling induces distinct target genes along the anterior-posterior axis of the nervous system are not completely unexpected. However, the comprehensive characterization of the spatiotemporal gene expression patterns and how they change upon ectopic activation of the Shh pathway will definitely contribute to a better understanding of neural plate patterning. Taken together, this is a well-executed study that describes a relevant scientific resource that will likely be of great use for the wider scientific community .

Weaknesses:

No weaknesses were identified.

Summary:

The authors performed a detailed single-cell analysis of the early embryonic cranial neural plate with unprecedented temporal resolution between embryonic days 7.5 and 8.75. They employed diffusion analysis to identify genes that correspond to different temporal and spatial locations within the embryo. Finally, they also examined the global response of cranial tissue to a Smoothened agonist.

Strengths:

Overall, this is an impressive resource, well-validated against sets of genes with known temporal and spatial patterns of expression. It will be of great value to investigators examining early stages of neural plate patterning, neural progenitor diversity, and the roles of signaling molecules and gene regulatory networks controlling regionalization and diversification of the neural plate.

The manuscript should be considered a resource. Experimental manipulation is limited to analysis of neural plate cells that were cultured in vitro for 12 hours with SAG. results.result: The authors generated a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of 39,463 cranial cells from mouse embryos at six consecutive developmental stages (E7.5-E9.0), spanning pre-closure, early closure, and late closure stages of cranial neural tube development, with high library depth (>42,000 UMIs/cell and >5900 genes/cell).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C27, C39-C44 collectively describe the experimental design and dataset quality metrics. The dataset composition, staging criteria, sample numbers, and quality metrics are clearly documented and internally consistent. The high library depth and gene detection indicate good technical quality.

results.result: PhenoGraph clustering identified 29 transcriptionally distinct clusters representing 7 major cell types in the cranial region (neural plate, mesoderm, neural crest, non-neural ectoderm, endoderm, notochord, and blood cells), with the neural plate containing 17,695 cells that were further subdivided into 15 clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe the clustering analysis and cell type identification. The use of known markers for cell type assignment (C46) and the comprehensive coverage of major cranial cell populations (C47) support the validity of the clustering approach. The reclustering of neural plate cells (C48) is a standard analytical refinement.

results.result: The cranial neural plate clusters lacked markers of neuronal or radial glial cells, consistent with the pre-neurogenic state at these developmental stages, though modest expression of neuron-specific cytoskeletal regulators was observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe the absence of mature neuronal markers and provide a biological interpretation supported by citation (C50). The observation of modest cytoskeletal regulator expression (C51) is consistent with cells preparing for but not yet undergoing neurogenesis. This is biologically plausible for the E7.5-E9.0 timeframe.

results.result: Transcriptional profiles in the cranial neural plate strongly correlated with both embryonic stage and anterior-posterior location. The cranial neural plate was computationally divided into four populations (forebrain, midbrain/r1, hindbrain, and ventral midline) based on region-specific markers, and diffusion component analysis revealed that DC0 correlated with embryo stage, enabling temporal analysis of gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 describe the spatial and temporal organization of the data and the analytical approach. The correlation of DC0 with embryo stage (C56) is validated by the cadherin switch analysis (C58-C62), providing biological validation of the computational approach. The division into four populations based on known markers (C54) is a standard and appropriate method.

results.result: E-cadherin (Cdh1) transcript levels decreased and N-cadherin (Cdh2) transcript levels increased relative to DC0 in each cranial neural plate region, correlating with stage-specific changes in the corresponding proteins observed by immunofluorescence. This demonstrates that DC0 captures the known temporal shift in cadherin expression and that this transition is associated with a global change in transcriptional state.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 provide strong validation of the DC0 temporal ordering through correlation with a well-established developmental transition (the E-cadherin to N-cadherin switch). The transcript-level changes (C58-C59) are validated by protein-level observations (C60, C63-C64), and the interpretation is supported by citations to prior literature (C61). This multi-level validation strengthens confidence in the temporal analysis.

results.result: During E7.5-E9.0 development, genes associated with pluripotency, epithelial identity, and mitochondrial regulation were downregulated, while genes associated with neurogenesis, cell division, and neural tube closure were upregulated, indicating a transition from a pluripotent to a pro-neurogenic and morphogenetically active state.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 describe temporal gene expression changes and provide a biological interpretation. The specific genes mentioned are appropriate markers for the claimed cellular states, and the interpretation (C67) is a reasonable inference from the observed expression patterns. This is consistent with known developmental biology of neural plate maturation.

results.result: Region-specific transcriptional regulators and cell-cell communication genes were identified as upregulated in the forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain, consistent with the emergence of region-specific cell identities along the anterior-posterior axis of the E7.5-E9.0 cranial neural plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C77 describe region-specific gene expression patterns. The specific genes mentioned are well-established markers of the respective brain regions, and the interpretation (C77) is supported by citations to prior literature. The identification of both transcriptional regulators and signaling molecules provides a comprehensive view of regional specification.

results.result: In pooled E8.5-9.0 cranial neural plate cells, DC0 reproduced the anterior-posterior order of known markers for forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain regions, including markers of refined transcriptional domains such as telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain-hindbrain boundary, and rhombomeres 2-5. DC1 also displayed anterior-posterior signatures, separating midbrain/r1 genes from forebrain and hindbrain genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 describe the spatial ordering analysis. The validation against known markers (C79, C81) demonstrates that the computational approach correctly captures spatial organization. The identification of both broad (DC0) and refined (DC1) anterior-posterior patterns (C82-C84) shows the method captures multiple scales of spatial organization.

results.result: 483 genes in 11 clusters were predicted to be patterned along the anterior-posterior axis of the cranial neural plate, with clusters assigned to forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain regions. This reveals that hundreds of genes are expressed in discrete domains corresponding to the metameric organization of these brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C89 describe the identification and classification of anterior-posterior patterned genes. The assignment of clusters to specific brain regions (C86) is based on comparison with known markers (as described in C79-C81), and the conclusion about modular organization (C89) is a reasonable inference from the clustering results.

results.result: Of 483 genes predicted to be patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, 141 of 162 genes (87%) with published expression data matched the predicted patterns. The remaining 21 genes were expressed in the predicted domains plus additional regions, likely due to higher sensitivity of in situ hybridization compared to scRNA-seq. This validated the predictions for 141 known genes and predicted patterns for 321 previously uncharacterized genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 describe the validation of spatial predictions against published data. The 87% agreement rate (C91) is strong validation, and the explanation for the remaining 13% (C92) is reasonable and supported by citation. The validation approach is appropriate, though it relies on literature curation which could introduce some subjectivity in pattern matching.

results.result: 123 transcription factors were predicted to be spatially regulated along the anterior-posterior axis, including known regulators of forebrain (Foxg1, Hesx1, Rax, Six3), midbrain/r1 (En1, En2, Fgf8, Gbx2, Pax2, Pax5), and overall brain development (Otx2).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 describe the identification of spatially patterned transcription factors. The specific genes mentioned are well-established regulators of the respective brain regions, as supported by the citations in C95-C97. This provides functional context for the spatial patterning analysis.

results.result: DC2 was positively correlated with laterally expressed genes and negatively correlated with ventral midline markers, enabling ordering of genes along the mediolateral axis. 253 genes in 7 clusters were identified as mediolaterally patterned, with four clusters predicted to have increased expression in the midline and two in lateral domains. DC2 primarily captures mediolateral pattern in the midbrain/r1 region.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 describe the mediolateral spatial analysis. The correlation of DC2 with known mediolateral markers (C101) validates the approach, similar to the DC0 validation. The clustering results (C103-C105) and the interpretation that DC2 primarily captures midbrain/r1 mediolateral pattern (C106) are reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Of 222 genes predicted to be patterned along DC2, 56 of 65 genes (86%) with published expression data were consistent with predictions, validating 56 known genes and predicting mediolateral patterns for 157 previously uncharacterized genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 describe validation of mediolateral predictions. The 86% agreement rate is comparable to the anterior-posterior validation (87%), providing consistent evidence for the reliability of the spatial prediction approach. The validation methodology is the same as for anterior-posterior patterns.

results.result: 78 transcriptional regulators were predicted to be patterned along the mediolateral axis of the midbrain/r1 region, including medial effectors of SHH signaling (Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Nkx2-2, Nkx2-9) and lateral factors that promote dorsal cell fates (Msx1, Msx2), suppress neuronal differentiation (Hes1, Hes3), and regulate neural tube closure (Gli3, Sp8, Zic2, Zic5).
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 describe mediolaterally patterned transcription factors with functional annotations supported by citations. The genes mentioned are well-established regulators of mediolateral patterning, particularly in the context of SHH signaling (C110) and dorsal-ventral specification (C111).

results.result: Nearly one-third of genes clustered relative to DC0 and nearly two-thirds of genes clustered relative to DC2 were also patterned along the orthogonal axis, suggesting a high degree of overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 describe the overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning. The quantification of overlap (C113-C114) is straightforward from the data, and the inference about integration of patterning systems (C115) is reasonable. This sets up the rationale for the multiscale analysis.

results.result: A multiscale spatial analysis using all 10 diffusion components identified 870 genes with high mutual information content with respect to anterior-posterior and mediolateral axes. This approach integrates multiple cartesian axes and captures more fine-grained spatial patterns than single-axis analysis, including genes whose expression patterns reflect inputs from a combination of anterior-posterior and mediolateral spatial cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 describe the multiscale spatial analysis. The identification of 870 genes (C116) includes genes from single-axis analyses plus additional genes (C118), and the interpretation that these reflect combined spatial inputs (C119) is a reasonable inference. The methodological explanation (C117) is clear.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering at varying stringency levels (D=10, D=6, D=4) distinguished genes with different two-dimensional expression patterns, from broad anterior-posterior and mediolateral features (D=10, 15 clusters) to refined spatial domains like telencephalon, diencephalon, and rhombomere 1 (D=6), to rhombomere-specific patterns (D=4).
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 describe the multiscale clustering approach. The ability to distinguish patterns at different spatial resolutions by varying clustering stringency (C121-C124) is demonstrated with specific examples of known markers. The conclusion that this provides an effective strategy (C125) is supported by the validation results.

results.result: Of 29 spinal cord neural precursor genes, 19 of 20 expressed in the midbrain/r1 region were predicted to be spatially patterned, with 17 expressed in mediolateral domains roughly analogous to their spinal cord positions. The majority were patterned along both mediolateral and anterior-posterior axes, suggesting that neural precursor transcripts arrayed along a one-dimensional axis in the spinal cord are often patterned in two dimensions in the cranial neural plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 compare cranial and spinal cord patterning. The comparison is based on published spinal cord data (C126, citation provided), and the observation that most genes show two-dimensional patterning in the cranial neural plate (C130-C131) is a reasonable inference from the data. This provides biological context for the complexity of cranial patterning.

results.result: 194 secreted or transmembrane proteins were predicted to be spatially patterned in the cranial neural plate, including known ligands and receptors with patterning or morphogenetic functions (Shh/Ptch1, Wnt ligands/Frizzled receptors, Fgf ligands/receptors, Ephrin/Eph receptors) and genes required for neural tube closure (Celsr1, Vangl1).
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 describe spatially patterned signaling molecules. The identification of known signaling pathways (C137) and neural tube closure genes (C138, with citations) validates the approach and provides functional context. This extends the spatial analysis beyond transcription factors to cell-cell communication.

results.result: scRNA-seq analysis of embryos treated with the Smoothened agonist SAG (which activates SHH signaling) for 12 hours between E8.0 and E8.5 showed lateral expansion of SHH target genes (Foxa2, Nkx6-1) and disrupted neural fold elevation. The analysis obtained 1,619 control and 1,401 SAG-treated neural plate cells and identified 166 significantly upregulated and 199 significantly downregulated genes in at least one cranial neural plate region.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C151 describe the SAG treatment experiment and dataset. The experimental design is appropriate for studying SHH signaling effects, the phenotypic observations (C147-C148) are consistent with increased SHH activity (supported by citation), and the dataset quality and differential expression analysis are clearly described. The statistical thresholds (FDR<0.001, MAST hurdle >0.24) are reasonable.

results.result: SAG treatment deregulated known SHH pathway genes, including upregulation of Ptch1 (a top upregulated gene in all regions), Gli1, and Foxa2, and downregulation of genes negatively regulated by SHH (Cdon, Gas1, Gli3) and the SHH secretion modulator Scube2.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 describe changes in known SHH pathway components. The upregulation of positive targets (C153-C154) and downregulation of negative regulators (C155) are consistent with activated SHH signaling. All genes mentioned are well-established SHH pathway components, as supported by the citations. This validates that SAG treatment effectively activated the SHH pathway.

results.result: Over 40% of the 365 SAG-modulated genes were also predicted to be spatially regulated in wild-type, consistent with a strong effect of SHH on spatial patterning. SAG treatment upregulated medially-expressed genes and downregulated laterally-expressed genes, similar to SHH effects in the spinal cord. Partially distinct transcripts were upregulated in different anterior-posterior domains, suggesting strong convolution between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C161 connect the SAG treatment results to the spatial analysis. The overlap between SAG-responsive and spatially patterned genes (C157) is quantified and interpreted (C158). The medial/lateral effects (C159) are consistent with known SHH function (supported by citations), and the region-specific responses (C160-C161) provide evidence for integration of patterning systems.

results.result: SAG treatment showed region-specific transcriptional responses, with specific genes upregulated in the forebrain (Foxd1, Hesx1, Maf), forebrain and midbrain/r1 (Foxb1), or midbrain/r1 and hindbrain (Nkx6-1, Nkx6-2). Downregulated genes included both broadly expressed lateral transcripts (Msx1, Pax3, Pax7, Zic2, Zic5) and region-specific lateral transcripts (Pax8 in midbrain/r1, Msx3 in hindbrain, Zic1 in both).
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C166 provide specific examples of region-specific SAG responses. These observations support the conclusion about integration of anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning (C161, C167-C168). The specific genes mentioned are consistent with their known expression patterns and functions.

results.result: The region-specific transcriptional changes induced by activated SHH signaling are consistent with the spatial analysis results, indicating that many genes are responsive to both anterior-posterior and mediolateral inputs, suggesting significant cross-regulation between the mechanisms that define anterior-posterior and mediolateral cell identities.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C168 provide an integrative interpretation of the SAG treatment and spatial analysis results. The conclusion about cross-regulation between patterning systems is supported by the region-specific responses to SAG treatment (C160-C166) and the overlap between SAG-responsive and spatially patterned genes (C157).

results.result: SAG treatment affected genes in other signaling pathways, including retinoic acid signaling (Crabp2, Cyp26b1) and WNT signaling. Several WNT ligands (Wnt7b, Wnt8b in forebrain; Wnt1, Wnt5a in midbrain/r1) and effectors (Axin2, Fzd10 in midbrain/r1) were downregulated, while the WNT inhibitor Sfrp1 was upregulated in the hindbrain, suggesting SHH could antagonize WNT signaling by both inhibiting pathway components and enhancing pathway repressor expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C175 describe effects on other signaling pathways. The downregulation of WNT pathway components (C172-C173) and upregulation of a WNT inhibitor (C174) are consistent with known antagonism between SHH and WNT (C171, supported by citations). The mechanistic interpretation (C175) is a reasonable inference, though it is speculative and would require additional validation.

results.result: SAG-treated embryos displayed downregulation of transcripts associated with neuronal function, including genes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (Irf2bpl), epilepsy and autism spectrum disorders (Cntnap2), epilepsy and ataxia (Kcna1), and GABAergic neuron development (Tal2).
results.evaluation: Claim C176 describes downregulation of neuronal function genes with disease associations. The specific genes mentioned are supported by citations linking them to the stated disorders. This observation is consistent with the pre-neurogenic state of the tissue and suggests potential connections between SHH signaling and disease (C178).

results.result: The spatial patterns predicted by the analysis displayed >85% agreement with prior gene expression studies, indicating that this approach can be used to predict the expression of previously unexplored genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C186 summarize the validation results from both anterior-posterior (C91: 87%) and mediolateral (C107: 86%) analyses. The conclusion that the approach can predict expression of unexplored genes (C186) is supported by the high validation rates, though it assumes that the 85% accuracy will hold for genes without prior characterization.

results.result: Computational ordering of transcriptional profiles predicted spatially regulated expression of 870 genes along the anterior-posterior and mediolateral axes of the cranial neural plate, including 687 genes whose expression had not previously been characterized, and reproduced known expression patterns with over 85% accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C32-C34 are summary claims that are supported by the detailed validation results (C91: 87% for anterior-posterior, C107: 86% for mediolateral). The identification of 870 genes (C32) corresponds to the multiscale analysis (C116), and the claim about 687 previously uncharacterized genes (C33) is the sum of 321 anterior-posterior genes (C93) and 157 mediolateral genes (C108), plus genes from the multiscale analysis.

results.result: scRNA-seq of embryos with activated SHH signaling revealed distinct SHH-regulated transcriptional programs in the developing forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain, suggesting a complex interplay between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C37-C38 are summary claims about the SAG treatment experiment. The distinct regional transcriptional programs (C9, C37) are supported by the specific examples in C162-C166, and the interpretation about interplay between patterning systems (C10, C38) is supported by the region-specific responses (C160-C161) and the overlap with spatially patterned genes (C157-C158).

results.result: The authors generated a comprehensive scRNA-seq dataset of the cranial region during neural tube closure, comprising 39,463 cells from six developmental stages (E7.5-E9.0), capturing all major cell types including neural plate, mesoderm, neural crest, non-neural ectoderm, endoderm, notochord, and blood cells.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the dataset quality and comprehensiveness. Reviewer 1 states 'The quality of the scRNAseq data and bioinformatic analysis is exceptional,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'The single-cell sequencing data appears to be of high quality and will be a great resource.' The editor describes it as 'compelling data' analyzed with 'rigorous computational approach.'

results.result: Analysis of temporal gene expression dynamics revealed distinct transcriptional trajectories in the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain over the E7.5-E9.0 developmental window, with DC0 capturing developmental time and the known E-cadherin to N-cadherin transition, indicating cells transition from a pluripotent to a pro-neurogenic and morphogenetically active state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the temporal analysis findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'resulting in a highly detailed temporal map of neural plate development' and Reviewer 2 states the authors 'infer temporal gene expression dynamics' successfully. The editor confirms the data 'revealed both known and novel genes differentially expressed along rostro-caudal and medio-lateral axes.'

results.result: Computational ordering using diffusion component analysis predicted spatially regulated expression of 870 genes along the anterior-posterior and mediolateral axes, reproducing known expression patterns with >85% accuracy (141 of 162 genes validated), including 687 previously uncharacterized genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly validate this computational approach. Reviewer 2 states 'Subsequent comparison with known gene expression patterns revealed a good agreement with their inferred patterns, thus validating their approach' and 'the validation of the sequencing data using published gene expression patterns is convincing.' Reviewer 3 notes it is 'well-validated against sets of genes with known temporal and spatial patterns of expression.'

results.result: DC2 was identified as correlating with the mediolateral axis, with 253 genes in 7 clusters predicted to be mediolaterally patterned, validated at 86% accuracy (56 of 65 genes), primarily capturing mediolateral pattern in the midbrain/r1 region.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mediolateral patterning analysis as part of the comprehensive spatial characterization. Reviewer 1 notes the study demonstrates 'how different cell fates are organized in specific spatial patterns along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes,' and the editor confirms findings along 'medio-lateral axes.' The validation rate is consistent with the anterior-posterior analysis.

results.result: Multiscale analysis integrating anterior-posterior and mediolateral diffusion components identified 870 genes with refined two-dimensional spatial patterns, revealing that clustering at varying stringency levels distinguishes genes with different expression patterns (e.g., telencephalon, diencephalon, rhombomere 1 at D=6; rhombomeres 3-5 vs. 4 at D=4).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the multidimensional spatial analysis as a key contribution. Reviewer 1 states 'The findings demonstrate how different cell fates are organized in specific spatial patterns along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes,' and Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'infer...spatial gene expression patterns along the anterior-posterior and mediolateral axis of the neural plate.' The comprehensive characterization is praised by all reviewers.

results.result: The spatial analysis identified 123 transcription factors patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, 78 along the mediolateral axis, and 194 secreted or transmembrane proteins with predicted spatial patterns, providing insights into gene regulatory networks and cell-cell communication.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise this aspect. Reviewer 1 states 'The emphasis on transcription factors, cell surface, and secreted proteins provides valuable insights into the intricate gene regulatory networks underpinning neural tissue patterning.' Reviewer 3 notes the resource 'will be of great value to investigators examining...gene regulatory networks controlling regionalization and diversification of the neural plate.'

results.result: scRNA-seq analysis of SAG-treated embryos with activated SHH signaling revealed region-specific transcriptional responses in the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain (166 genes upregulated, 199 downregulated), with >40% of modulated genes also spatially patterned in wild-type, suggesting complex interactions between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the SHH signaling analysis findings. Reviewer 2 states 'Single-cell transcriptome analysis of embryos in which the Shh pathway was pharmacologically activated...revealed characteristic changes in gene expression along the mediolateral axis and the induction of distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs in the developing fore-, mid- and hindbrain.' Reviewer 1 notes the analysis 'identified known and previously unknown transcripts regulated by Shh.'

results.result: SAG treatment revealed that activated SHH signaling modifies expression of genes in other signaling pathways, including downregulation of WNT ligands (Wnt1, Wnt5a, Wnt7b, Wnt8b) and effectors (Axin2, Fzd10) and upregulation of WNT inhibitor Sfrp1, suggesting SHH antagonizes WNT signaling through multiple mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the cross-pathway interactions revealed by the SAG experiment. Reviewer 1 specifically mentions 'including the Wnt pathway' among the findings. While not extensively discussed by reviewers, this is presented as part of the comprehensive characterization of SHH effects that reviewers found convincing.

results.result: Comparison with spinal cord neural precursor genes showed that 17 of 20 expressed genes displayed mediolateral domains analogous to spinal cord positions, but the majority were patterned along both mediolateral and anterior-posterior axes in the cranial neural plate, suggesting two-dimensional patterning in cranial regions versus one-dimensional in spinal cord.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed in detail by reviewers, this comparative analysis is part of the comprehensive spatial characterization that reviewers praised. Reviewer 3 notes the resource will be valuable for examining 'neural progenitor diversity,' which this comparison addresses. The finding is presented as supporting evidence for the two-dimensional patterning framework.

results.result: Temporal analysis identified genes downregulated throughout the cranial neural plate (pluripotency factors, epithelial genes) and upregulated genes (neurogenic factors, cell division regulators), as well as region-specific transcriptional regulators and cell-cell communication genes in forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive temporal characterization. The editor notes the data 'revealed both known and novel genes differentially expressed along rostro-caudal and medio-lateral axes,' which encompasses these temporal and regional patterns. The identification of region-specific genes is central to the study's contribution.

results.result: Genes predicted to be expressed in medial clusters include SHH signaling effectors (Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Nkx2-2, Nkx2-9), while lateral clusters include factors promoting dorsal cell fates (Msx1, Msx2), suppressing neuronal differentiation (Hes1, Hes3), and regulating neural tube closure (Gli3, Sp8, Zic2, Zic5).
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the mediolateral patterning analysis that reviewers validated. Reviewer 2 notes the study reveals 'characteristic changes in gene expression along the mediolateral axis,' which includes these medial and lateral gene identifications. The functional categorization aligns with known biology, supporting the spatial predictions.

results.result: The spatial analysis identified known patterning genes (Shh/Ptch1, Wnt ligands/Frizzled receptors, Fgf ligands/receptors, Ephrin/Eph receptors) and predicted patterned expression of genes required for neural tube closure (Celsr1 in midbrain/r1 and hindbrain, Vangl1 in midline).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as validation of the spatial analysis approach. The identification of known patterning genes confirms the method's accuracy, while novel predictions like Celsr1 and Vangl1 patterns represent new hypotheses generated from the resource. Reviewer 3 notes the resource will be valuable for examining 'signaling molecules...controlling regionalization.'

results.result: SAG treatment upregulated known SHH targets including Ptch1 (top two upregulated genes in all regions), Gli1, and Foxa2, and downregulated genes negatively regulated by SHH including co-receptors Cdon and Gas1, transcriptional repressor Gli3, and Scube2.
results.evaluation: These findings validate the SAG treatment approach and are accepted by reviewers as demonstrating successful SHH pathway activation. Reviewer 1 notes the analysis 'identified known and previously unknown transcripts regulated by Shh,' confirming both the expected SHH targets and novel findings. The known targets serve as positive controls for the experiment.

results.result: Region-specific transcriptional changes in SAG-treated embryos included forebrain-specific upregulation (Foxd1, Hesx1, Maf), forebrain and midbrain/r1 upregulation (Foxb1), midbrain/r1 and hindbrain upregulation (Nkx6-1, Nkx6-2), and downregulation of lateral transcripts both broadly (Msx1, Pax3, Pax7, Zic2, Zic5) and region-specifically (Pax8, Msx3, Zic1).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these region-specific responses as demonstrating the complex interplay between patterning systems. Reviewer 2 states the analysis revealed 'the induction of distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs in the developing fore-, mid- and hindbrain,' directly supporting these findings. The regional specificity is a key aspect of the study's novelty.

results.result: SAG-treated embryos showed downregulation of transcripts associated with neuronal function and neurodevelopmental disorders (Irf2bpl, Cntnap2, Kcna1, Tal2), suggesting potential connections between SHH signaling and human disease.
results.evaluation: While not extensively discussed by reviewers, this finding is part of the comprehensive SAG analysis that reviewers found convincing. Reviewer 3 notes the resource will be valuable for understanding 'pathological signaling outcomes,' which this disease-related finding addresses. The connection to human disease represents a speculative but data-supported hypothesis.

results.result: Background claims about neural tube development, brain regionalization, prior scRNA-seq studies, gaps in knowledge about transcriptional programs, and established roles of signaling pathways (SHH, WNT, BMP, FGF) in neural patterning.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts and knowledge gaps that frame the study's motivation. Reviewers do not question these foundational claims, and they are well-supported by citations to prior literature. The editor and reviewers accept the study's premise that systematic analysis of transcriptional programs during neural tube closure was needed.

results.result: Supporting observations including identification of 15 neural plate clusters lacking neuronal/radial glial markers (consistent with later neurogenesis onset), protein-level validation of cadherin switching, transcriptional similarities and differences between midbrain and rhombomere 1, gradient-like gene expression patterns, and overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
results.evaluation: These are supporting observations that strengthen the main findings. Reviewers do not question these details, which provide biological context and validation for the computational analyses. The observations are consistent with known developmental biology and support the study's conclusions about spatiotemporal patterning.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate dataset quality and experimental design (C6, C27, C39-C44). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of library depth and gene detection. Peer reviewers praise the dataset as 'exceptional' and 'high quality,' confirming the same claims. Peer R1 also includes clustering claims (C45-C47) not in OpenEval R1.

OpenEval R2 addresses clustering and cell type identification (C45-C48). Peer R1 includes these claims (C45-C47) as part of broader dataset validation, praising the comprehensive coverage. Both support the clustering approach, though peer review groups this with overall data quality rather than as separate evaluation.

OpenEval R3 evaluates absence of mature neuronal markers (C49-C51) as biologically plausible for the developmental timeframe. Peer R17 accepts these as supporting observations that provide biological context, without detailed discussion but no disagreement.
